title: Everything Everywhere All At Once, Sisyphus Perfected

commenti.body:
I can’t argue it hasn’t got a style, I just think everything being so over the top only works up to a certain point. I appreciate the media/sensory overload is part of the film, but it seemed like a rather trite one that they hammer you with for the entirety.

I essentially like the message of the film but the delivery to me just didn’t work. You can see every single joke coming a mile off, and the emotional moments similarly were so heavily sign-posted that there seemed to be little room for interpretation or subtext.

I really wanted to like it but found myself audibly groaning when I realised the ‘part 3’ title screen was real and there was still a third of this film left. I think my next overall opinion is swayed slightly by all the rabid praise for the film, which definitely affected my expectations. 

I guess I missed out on the portion relating directly to the Asian/immigrant experience which I understand is quite powerful.

There’s no way to say this without sounding like a complete snob, but this film being ‘deep’ makes a lot more sense to me mostly in comparison to the mainstream churn of superhero movies and comedies with philosophical/existential themes just tacked on.

It's fundamentally a genre film. It is, at it's nature, a philosophical *kung fu* movie similar to Crouching Tiger or Enter The Dragon. However, the triviality is part of the absurd. It's a point. Everything is trivial. As Camus inelegantly put it "I can either kill myself or have a cup of coffee." There's no point looking past the surface in an absurdist world of one desires happiness. To do so is to suffer.

This "don't look too deep" messaging is rather literal in the film with the bagel. It's staring into it that leads to destruction. Looking past it's surface and trying to define it that is dangerous. "Letting go" and just embracing the absurd is the answer to happiness.

Nothing matters, so just live in the now.
